title: Rama is dharma with a body
hook: flatterers are everywhere, says an old rakshasa to his king; the person who tells you the hard truth is rare

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha talked Ravana out of the plan, until Shurpanakha shamed him in his court. Ahankara, the pride that Dussehra burns.

Ravana sets out again in his flying chariot, along the coast. Valmiki slows down to paint it: shores lined with coconut palms and sandalwood, pearls drying on the beaches, hermitages of sages, and merchants' ships. Then the chariot lands at Maricha's hermitage a second time. The old rakshasa, in bark clothes and matted hair, welcomes his king with food and water, and asks, carefully: why have you come back?
screen: `A FLYING CHARIOT ALONG THE COAST.` → `PEARLS ON THE BEACHES.` → `WHY HAVE YOU COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Ravana spells out the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer, spotted with silver, and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want you. Rama and Lakshmana will go after you. Then I'll take her. Maricha begins with a saying: people who say pleasant things are always easy to find, king. But someone who says what is unpleasant and good for you, and someone who will listen to it, those are rare. Then he tells Ravana the truth he doesn't want. You don't know who Rama is. He wasn't sent to the forest for any crime; he went to keep his father's word. And then a short line in Sanskrit: ramo vigrahavan dharmah. Rama is dharma in bodily form. To steal his wife is to walk into a fire. Look at who's speaking: not a sage, not a friend, but a rakshasa, Rama's old enemy, once hurled across the sea by him. Even his enemy saw it. Hold on to that line, because it's how Hindus learn dharma. Dharma is a big word: right living, duty, truth, the order that holds the world together. It's hard to learn from a definition. So the tradition gives you a person. When a child asks what dharma looks like, many Hindu families point to Rama: keeping his father's word, faithful to Sita, protecting the sages, warning his enemies before he fights. You don't memorize dharma. You watch it, and walk after it.
screen: `BECOME A GOLDEN DEER.` · `PLEASANT WORDS ARE EASY TO FIND.` · `RAMA IS DHARMA IN BODILY FORM.` · `EVEN HIS ENEMY SAW IT.` · then, large: `DHARMA HAS A BODY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who told you something you didn't want to hear that turned out to be true and good for you, the rare kind Maricha talks about. Picture their face as they said it, and notice what it cost them. Let a little gratitude rise. If you can, send them a short thank-you text after the sit.
Dharma: right living, duty, truth. Maricha tells his king that flatterers are easy to find, and that Rama is dharma in bodily form.
Hold on to it: dharma has a body, and it's Rama. The rare friend says the hard thing, and the rare listener hears it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Maricha's line ramo vigrahavan dharmah, Rama is dharma in bodily form, is quoted on its own in Hindu teaching, as are his lines on rare, honest advice.

original.note: Sanskrit: 'Rama is dharma with a body,' Maricha's line in Aranya 37.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maricha is just Ravana's helper.
what it means: he warns Ravana, and calls Rama dharma itself: the person Hindus look to when they ask what dharma looks like.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 37 holds both the verse on rare honest advice and 'ramo vigrahavan dharmah', two lines that stand on their own as sayings.
